faq.a: Poteho makes premium pet supplies: carriers, beds, apparel, leashes and feeding gear for retailers and brands in 30+ countries, with low MOQ and custom branding.

faq.q: Why choose Poteho as a pet products supplier?
faq.a: Since 2020 we have combined in-house QC, flexible MOQs, OEM/ODM customization and worldwide shipping, treating every order, large or small, with care.

posts.title: A pet travel backpack that doesn't turn every outing into a workout
posts.excerpt: I learned what a bad carrier feels like on a train platform in Lisbon. My terrier was fine, the weather was fine, and I was the one struggling — one strap diggi
body: I learned what a bad carrier feels like on a train platform in Lisbon. My terrier was fine, the weather was fine, and I was the one struggling — one strap digging into my shoulder, the bag swinging every time I stepped around someone, and a low, steady ache settling into my back. We made it to the hotel. I spent the rest of the evening deciding the carrier was the problem, not the dog. A good pet travel backpack should be the opposite of that trip: something you forget you are wearing until you need to take it off.
## The weight is the whole game

People shop for a travel backpack by counting pockets. I wish they would start with weight instead, because that is what you actually feel after thirty minutes. There are two numbers that matter: how much the empty bag weighs, and where that weight sits once your pet is inside. A light bag that hangs away from your spine will still tire you out, because your shoulder muscles have to work to pull the load back toward your body. A slightly heavier bag with a flat, padded back panel can feel better, because it lets the weight settle over your hips and spine where it belongs.

Try this at home before you buy anything. Load the bag with a bag of rice roughly your pet's weight, put it on, and walk around your house for ten minutes. Ten minutes is enough to tell you everything. If one strap starts sliding off, if the bag bounces when you turn, or if you find yourself hunching, put it back. The strap adjustment is another thing people skip. A proper travel pack has straps you can tighten without the whole bag shifting, plus a chest clip that stops the straps from spreading. That little clip does more for comfort than any amount of extra padding.
## Ventilation you can actually see

Mesh panels sound like a box-ticking feature until you meet a dog who pants hard in warm weather. Then you start noticing where the openings are, not just how many there are. Side airflow helps, but the top matters more than most buyers expect. Heat rises. A closed top on a sunny day turns the bag into a small oven, and a dog who cannot cool themselves will get distressed fast. Look for a bag with breathable material across the upper section, not just a token strip of mesh on one side.

I also pay attention to whether the mesh is easy to see through from the pet's side. Dogs who can watch what is happening are usually calmer than dogs who sit in a dark box listening to a world they cannot see. That is one of the reasons we kept the mesh high on the body of the [Pet Carrier Backpack](/products/pth-1101.html) and left the top breathable — not because it photographs well, but because it is the difference between a dog who rides quietly and a dog who whines the whole way.
## What fold-flat really buys you

Here is a truth nobody mentions in product descriptions: most carriers spend ninety percent of their life folded under a bed or shoved into a car boot. They do not live in your hallway. So the ability to fold down flat is not a minor convenience, it is the feature that decides whether the bag ends up in a cupboard or gets donated to a charity shop after two trips.

Our bag folds to 36 x 32 x 7 cm, which is thin enough to slide behind a suitcase or under a car seat. That matters on the days when you are travelling with more than one animal, or when your hotel room is smaller than the photo suggested. The fabric is oxford cloth with a polyester lining — a combination that is light, wipes clean after a muddy walk, and does not hold smells the way some cheaper synthetics do. The whole thing weighs about 1 kg empty. Add a small dog and you are still well under what a hard carrier weighs before the pet goes in.

It comes in khaki and grey. I know that sounds like the least interesting sentence in this article, until you are choosing a bag that will spend half its life on public transport, in waiting rooms, and on pavements. Neutral colours hide the dust. Bright white looks lovely for about one outing. That is the entire design logic, and I make no apology for it.
## Getting your pet to actually go in

The best backpack in the world is useless if your cat treats it like a trap. This is where most people give up too early. They bring the bag out on the day of the appointment, coax, bribe, chase, and then conclude that their pet 'hates carriers'. What the pet actually hates is the sequence: bag appears, scary thing happens. You have to break that association before you need the bag.

Start by leaving it open in a room your pet already likes. Put a blanket or an old t-shirt of yours inside — something that smells familiar. Feed a treat near it, then just inside the opening, then further in over a few days. Do not zip it up yet. Let them go in and out freely, and let them decide. Once they are willing to sit inside for a minute, zip it for five seconds, unzip, and give a treat. Build from there over a week. The goal is not that your pet loves the bag. The goal is that the bag is boring.

Dogs usually need less convincing but more structure. Teach a 'go to your place' cue using the carrier as the place, and reward heavily at the beginning. If you only ever use the backpack when you are leaving the house, your dog will learn that the backpack predicts being taken somewhere, and enthusiasm will turn into resistance. Mix it up. Sometimes the backpack means a treat and a nap. Sometimes it means a short walk around the block. Predictability is useful, but so is the occasional pleasant surprise.
## The details that survive daily use

After a few months, you stop caring about how the bag looks and start caring about which parts are still working. The zip is usually the first failure point, so run it back and forth a few times before you buy and feel whether it catches. The strap stitching is the second. Look at where the straps meet the bag — that junction takes the whole load, and flimsy stitching there will let go long before the fabric wears through.

Cleaning is easier than people fear. Most of the time a damp cloth on the interior lining is enough. For anything more serious, take the removable mat out and wash it separately, and let the bag air dry fully before storing it. Never put a carrier away damp; you will know why the first time you open it a week later. Check the mesh for small snags too. A claw can catch a thread and turn it into a run, and a hole you barely notice is an escape route a determined cat will find.
## Planes, trains and the long walk home

Different journeys ask different things of a carrier. On a plane, the constraint is the seat in front — the bag has to fit underneath, which means soft sides and a little give are an advantage, even though we built ours for the more general case. On a train, you care more about whether the bag stays upright when the carriage rocks and whether the door can be opened one-handed while you are standing. On foot, it all comes back to strap comfort and weight.

Whichever you are doing, take a rehearsal trip before the real one. Walk to the end of your street with the bag on. Sit in a cafe with it under the table. See how your pet settles when you stop moving, because that is when animals tend to get restless. You will learn more in one rehearsal than in an hour of reading reviews, and you will learn it while you are still close enough to home to turn around.
## A few things I now pack without thinking

Over time I have settled on a small routine that makes carrier trips smoother. A collapsible water bowl and a bottle that fits in the side pocket mean I am not hunting for a café every time my dog gets thirsty. A poop bag roll clipped to the strap has saved me more than once. I also carry a small towel, because a dog who has been sitting in a carrier for an hour can come out with a damp coat, and a quick wipe before they go back on the furniture prevents an argument at home. None of this is about the bag itself. It is about the fact that a good carrier gives you the freedom to stay out longer, and staying out longer means you need a little system.

One more habit: I check the bag the night before any trip. Not a thorough inspection — just a pull on each strap, a run of the zip, and a look at the mesh for anything that has snagged since last time. Two minutes at home is infinitely better than discovering a stuck zip at a station with a dog on a lead in one hand and a suitcase in the other. Travel with a pet is mostly a series of small preparations like this. The carrier is simply the piece that holds them all together.

So if you are shopping for a pet travel backpack, ignore the pocket count. Test the straps, look at the top, check how small it folds, and give yourself a week to make the bag feel ordinary. Do those four things and the next train platform will be a much calmer place.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [Looking at a Carhartt dog jacket? Here's what to compare before you buy](/blog/looking-at-a-carhartt-dog-jacket-compare-this.html), [Living with a torn ACL: what a leg brace can and can't do](/blog/living-with-a-torn-acl-what-a-brace-can-do.html), ['Airline approved' is not a stamp — here's what to check](/blog/airline-approved-is-not-a-stamp.html).

faq.q: Are pet travel backpacks allowed on planes?
faq.a: It depends on the airline and the aircraft. Most airlines accept a soft-sided backpack that fits under the seat in front, but the exact dimensions vary. Check your airline's pet policy before booking, measure the outside of the bag including any protruding parts, and choose a bag that can squash down slightly at the gate.

faq.q: How do I get my cat to accept a backpack carrier?
faq.a: Leave it open in a room they like with familiar-smelling bedding inside. Feed treats near it, then inside it, over several days. Once they go in willingly, zip it for a few seconds at a time and build up slowly. Never force the first trip — a carrier associated with fear is much harder to fix later.

faq.q: How much weight can a backpack carrier hold?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer's stated limit rather than guessing. The PTH-1101 is designed for small dogs and cats; the useful test is whether your pet can stand, turn around and lie down comfortably. If your pet fills the bag completely, size up rather than relying on the weight rating alone.

posts.title: Why I stopped holding the leash on morning runs
posts.excerpt: For years I ran with the leash looped over one hand and my phone in the other. It worked right up until it didn't — a sudden squirrel, a tightened grip, and a j
body: For years I ran with the leash looped over one hand and my phone in the other. It worked right up until it didn't — a sudden squirrel, a tightened grip, and a jolt that went straight through my wrist. I came home more sore from the leash than from the run. Worse, I had spent the whole route bracing for the next pull instead of paying attention to where we were going. That is a strange way to enjoy a morning.
## What 'hands free' actually changes

A hands free dog leash moves the connection point from your hand to your waist. That sounds like a small change and it is not. The difference is balance. When the pull comes from a belt around your hips, your arms stay loose, your shoulders stay down, and your stride stays normal. You stop acting as an anchor and start moving as a pair. For anyone who runs with a dog who is stronger than them, or just more enthusiastic, this changes the whole experience.

There is a learning curve, and I should be honest about it. The first week I kept reaching down for a handle that wasn't there. I also over-corrected at corners, because I was not used to steering with my hips rather than my hand. By the second week it clicked. I had my phone in one hand and water in the other, my dog settled into a rhythm beside me, and the run felt like a run again rather than a negotiation.

The other thing nobody tells you: a waist leash gives your dog more consistent feedback. When you hold a lead, your grip tightens and loosens without you noticing. The signal your dog receives is unpredictable. A belt-mounted connection stays at the same height and same tension, which makes it easier for a dog to learn where 'too far' is. Consistency is the whole basis of good lead manners, and this setup gives you more of it for free.
## The reflective stripe matters more than you think

Most people buy a running leash for the walk, then use it at six in the morning in January when it is still properly dark. A reflective stripe stitched along the length does nothing for your dog directly. What it does is make the two of you visible as one object, at roughly hip height, which is exactly where a driver's headlights are pointing. A reflective collar on a low dog can disappear behind a kerb. A stripe along a leash that runs up to your waist cannot.

Check how the reflective material is applied, though. Printed-on silver looks bright in a product photo but rubs off after a few months of cable-style movement against your leg. Stitched reflective thread lasts far longer. Our [Pet Running Leash](/products/pth-1402.html) has the stripe integrated into the webbing instead of printed on top, for exactly this reason. It costs a little more to make and it is the one upgrade I would never skip for a city dog.
## Where a waist leash does not belong

I still use a short standard lead in crowds, at busy crossings, and around other dogs. A hands free setup gives you less precise control in tight spaces, and pretending otherwise is how someone gets tripped. If your dog lunges at passing cyclists, a belt-mounted leash means the reaction happens faster than you can unclip. You cannot step on a leash that is attached to your waist, which is a technique most experienced walkers use without thinking.

The same goes for narrow pavements, slippery surfaces, and anywhere with a real drop. Keep a short lead in your pocket for those moments. A hands free leash is a tool for open routes — parks, canals, quiet streets, trails — not a universal replacement. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something.

There is also a simple physical limit. A waist leash works because your body weight is the counterweight. If your dog is large enough to move you rather than the other way round, no leash design will fix that. In that case, a front-clip harness and proper training come first, and the hands free leash comes later as a reward for good behaviour rather than a solution to bad behaviour.
## Choosing the right belt and length

Not all waist leashes are the same. The belt itself should be wide enough that it does not dig in, and it should stay put when you sprint. A narrow strap that rolls over itself is miserable after a kilometre. Look for a belt that can be adjusted while you are wearing it, because you will want to change the fit between a jacket in winter and a t-shirt in summer.

Length matters too. Too short and your dog is forced into your shadow, which is unpleasant for both of you. Too long and you get a bungee effect where your dog runs ahead, hits the end, and pulls you forward. The useful range for running is roughly one and a half to two metres of slack, enough for your dog to find a natural stride without disappearing around a corner. A bungee section can help absorb sudden pulls, but it also hides the tension signal your dog relies on, so I prefer a flat webbing lead with a bit of give in the material rather than an elastic insert.

The clip is worth checking as well. It is the single point of failure in the whole system. A cheap snap that sticks or has a weak gate will eventually open at the wrong moment. Run your thumb over it, open and close it a few times, and look for a proper swivel so the leash does not twist into a rope as your dog changes direction.
## Training your dog to walk on a waist leash

Do not start with a run. Start in your living room. Put the belt on, clip the leash, and stand still for a minute while you give your dog a treat for checking in with you. Then walk a few steps indoors. The novelty of the setup is interesting to a dog, and you want that interest associated with calm behaviour rather than with the excitement of leaving the house.

Move outside to a quiet street for the first few sessions. Keep the sessions short — five minutes is plenty. Reward your dog whenever the leash stays loose. If it goes tight, stop and wait rather than pulling. This is standard loose-lead training, but you are now doing it with your hands free, which means you have to notice the tension through your body instead of through your palm. That takes a few days to get used to.

Once your dog walks calmly on a short route, add distance gradually. Add speed last. A dog who is fine walking beside you on a waist leash can still find a run exciting enough to forget their manners, so build up from a slow jog rather than jumping straight into your usual pace. And keep treats in a pocket you can actually reach. This sounds obvious until you are standing on a street corner with a treat bag clipped to the waist belt you cannot open one-handed.
## Care, maintenance and when to replace it

A leash lives a hard life. It gets wet, muddy, dragged through gravel, and left in a hot car. Rinse the webbing after a salty or muddy run and let it dry before you coil it up. Check the stitching around the belt loops and the clip attachment every few weeks. Those are the two places where load concentrates, and fraying there is a clear signal to retire the leash.

Replace it sooner rather than later if you see damage. A leash is cheap compared to the alternative. Reflective material that has worn dull is another good reason — the safety feature has quietly stopped working even though the leash still looks fine in daylight. I keep an older one in the car as a spare and replace the main one each spring.
## What changed for my dog, not just for me

I spent the first week thinking about my own comfort and barely noticed what the leash was doing for my dog. Then I watched a clip of us running from a friend's phone. My dog was trotting at a steady distance, checking back every few seconds, and I was not constantly tightening and releasing my grip. To a dog, that difference is huge. A hand-held lead transmits every tiny movement of your wrist — the phone shift, the coffee sip, the scratch of an itch — and a sensitive dog reads each one as a possible signal. A waist connection filters all that noise out. What is left is a clean, consistent line of communication.

My dog also stopped trying to lead. When the person holding the lead is visibly bracing, some dogs take that as permission to pull, because the human has already conceded the tension. With the attachment at my waist and my arms free, the whole dynamic changed without me running a single formal training session. That is not magic — it is just fewer accidental signals. But it is a good reminder that a lot of lead problems are really handling problems in disguise.

If your morning run currently involves clenching a leash for three kilometres, try moving the attachment to your waist and giving yourself a week to adjust. You probably won't go back. Just remember the short lead in your pocket for the crossings — that one habit will save you more trouble than any feature on the leash itself.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [The lick sleeve I wish we had after our dog's surgery](/blog/the-lick-sleeve-i-wish-we-had-after-surgery.html), [A pet travel backpack that doesn't turn every outing into a workout](/blog/pet-travel-backpack-that-doesnt-hurt.html), [What to ask a pet supplies distributor before your first order](/blog/what-to-ask-a-pet-supplies-distributor.html).

faq.q: Are hands free leashes safe for strong dogs?
faq.a: They are safe for dogs who already walk reasonably on a lead. A strong puller can still take you off balance, so a waist leash is not a substitute for training. Pair it with a front-clip harness, work on loose-lead walking, and keep a short lead for crowded or narrow places.

faq.q: Can I use a hands free leash for hiking?
faq.a: Yes, on open trails where you want your hands free for poles or a map. Keep a short lead accessible for narrow paths, river crossings and steep descents, where close control matters more than convenience.

faq.q: How long should a running leash be?
faq.a: Roughly one and a half to two metres of slack gives most dogs enough room to settle into a natural stride without running ahead. Shorter leads are better for training and busy streets; much longer ones create a delayed tug that is unpleasant for both of you.

posts.title: A waterproof dog coat is really about the walk after the rain stops
posts.excerpt: The rain is not the problem. The problem is the twenty minutes after, when your dog is wet, the wind picks up, and you are walking home with an animal who has s
body: The rain is not the problem. The problem is the twenty minutes after, when your dog is wet, the wind picks up, and you are walking home with an animal who has suddenly decided they are done. I have done that walk more times than I can count — the slowed pace, the lifted paw, the look back toward the car. A good waterproof dog coat is less about staying dry in the downpour and more about staying warm and comfortable on the way back.
## Waterproof, water-resistant, and why the difference matters

Plenty of coats are water-resistant, which is not the same thing as waterproof. Water-resistant shrugs off a light drizzle and then soaks through after ten minutes of steady rain. Waterproof means the outer shell actually sheds water under sustained pressure — including the pressure of your dog lying down on damp ground, which is where a lot of coats quietly fail.

There is a third term you will see: three-proof. In practice it usually means water-resistant, wind-resistant and stain-resistant. It is a useful shorthand but not a guarantee, so look for what the shell is made of and how the seams are handled. Sewn seams create thousands of tiny holes, and a coat with unsealed seams will let water through at the stitching even if the fabric itself is excellent. For a winter dog coat, you want a shell that sheds rain and a construction that does not leak at the joins.
## Fill that still works when damp

Here is the part that matters most in a real winter. A coat is only warm because of the air trapped in its filling. Some cheap stuffing collapses into a flat, wet pancake the moment it gets damp, and then you have a dog wearing a cold, heavy sheet. Granular cotton fill is useful here because it holds its loft better when it picks up a little moisture, and it dries faster once you get home.

It will never be as light as a high-end down filling, and I would not pretend otherwise. But down has its own problem: when it gets properly wet, it loses almost all of its insulating value and takes an age to dry. For a dog who bounds through puddles without a second thought, that is a realistic failure mode. Granular cotton is the sensible compromise — a little heavier, a lot more forgiving. That is what we put in the [Winter Waterproof Dog Coat](/products/pth-1501.html), and it is a decision based on how dogs actually behave, not on what looks impressive on a spec sheet.
## Four legs means four places to fail

Human jackets have two arm holes. Dog coats have four leg openings, and every one of them is a place where wind can get in, where fabric can ride up, or where a determined dog can twist themselves free. Check the leg openings before you buy anything. They should be roomy enough that your dog can stride without the coat pulling at their shoulders, but snug enough that the garment stays put when they run.

A coat that rotates around the body is worse than no coat at all, because the twisted fabric rubs and the belly is left exposed. The fix is usually a combination of a proper chest strap and a back length that matches your dog. Measure from the base of the neck to the base of the tail, and around the widest part of the chest. Those two numbers tell you more than the breed on the size label ever will. Two dogs of the same breed can have completely different builds, especially if one of them is carrying a little extra winter weight.

Then there is the belly. Some four-leg designs cover the underside fully, which is warm but can be awkward for male dogs and for toilet breaks. Others leave the belly open, which is easier but lets cold air in from below. For most dogs in most climates, a generous chest panel with an open belly is the better trade — warm where it counts, without the fuss.
## Reflective details are not decoration

Winter walks happen in the dark. If your dog is low to the ground and dark coloured, they are almost invisible from a distance. A reflective strip on the coat will not make your dog safe on its own — nothing replaces a short lead near roads — but it gives drivers a chance to see you both earlier. I treat it as a non-negotiable feature in any coat bought between October and March.

Check where the strip sits. A band around the belly is hidden from most angles. A strip along the back or down both sides is visible from behind and from the side, which covers the situations you actually encounter on a walk. Again, stitched reflective material beats printed silver for longevity. It is a small detail that survives a whole season of mud.
## Measuring well — most people get this wrong

I have measured a lot of dogs for coats, and the most common mistake is measuring over a thick winter coat rather than the body underneath, or measuring while the dog is squirming and the tape has gone crooked. Do it on a calm dog, ideally after a walk when they are settled. Run the tape from the base of the neck — where the collar sits — to the base of the tail, not to the tip of the tail. Then measure the chest at its widest point, usually just behind the front legs.

If your dog is between sizes, the decision depends on their build. A broad, deep-chested dog usually needs the larger size even if the back length fits the smaller one, because the chest strap has to close comfortably. A lean, long-legged dog can often take the smaller size. When you first put the coat on, you should be able to slip two fingers between the fabric and your dog's body. Any tighter and you risk restricting movement and breathing.

Watch your dog's first reaction too. A dog who freezes, hunches, or tries to back out immediately is telling you the coat is uncomfortable, even if the measurements look right. Take it off, check for anything pulling at the armpits or the throat, and try the next size. Do not power through it. A coat your dog tolerates rather than enjoys is still useful; a coat they panic in is not.
## Washing, drying and making it last

A winter coat gets filthy. Mud, salt on pavements, and the general grime of a wet walk all end up in the shell. Most coats can be wiped down with a damp cloth after a walk, which handles the day-to-day mess. A full wash should be rare — once or twice a season is plenty — because frequent washing wears out water-repellent treatments faster than actual use does.

Use a gentle cycle and a mild detergent, never fabric softener, which leaves a film that interferes with water resistance. Hang it to dry completely before storing. A coat folded away damp will smell by autumn and may develop mildew in the fill. If the water resistance starts to fade after a season, a reproofing spray can bring the shell back, though you should test it on a small area first.

Check the straps and buckles at the same time. These take more abuse than the fabric, especially if your dog pulls while you are fastening them. A broken buckle in a car park is a miserable way to end a walk, and replacements are rarely available when you need them.
## Different dogs, different answers

A greyhound and a husky will not get the same value from a winter coat, and any sensible owner knows it. Thin-coated breeds, small dogs, seniors and dogs recovering from illness feel the cold early, often at temperatures where you are still comfortable in a jumper. A coat for these dogs is not a luxury. It is the difference between a dog who wants to go out and a dog who waits by the door. For a thick-coated northern breed, a coat can actually cause overheating if they are running hard, even in cold weather. Watch the dog, not the thermometer.

Puppies and older dogs need a little extra thought. Puppies have less body fat and poorer temperature regulation, so short coats and more frequent trips are better than one long walk in the cold. Older dogs often have thinner coats and slower circulation, and they feel damp and wind more than they used to. For both groups, the right coat is the one that lets them keep their normal routine without you having to cut the walk short. That is the measure I use now: not whether the coat looks good, but whether we still do the full loop.

When you are choosing a waterproof dog coat, think about the walk home. That is when you will be glad you bought one — when the rain has stopped, the wind has started, and your dog is still out there enjoying themselves while you are the one thinking about the warm kitchen. Get the fill and the fit right, and that walk becomes the best part of the day instead of the part you rush.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
