If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [What a blind dog halo actually does (and what it can't)](/blog/what-a-blind-dog-halo-actually-does.html), [Why I stopped holding the leash on morning runs](/blog/why-i-stopped-holding-the-leash-on-runs.html), [Looking at a Carhartt dog jacket? Here's what to compare before you buy](/blog/looking-at-a-carhartt-dog-jacket-compare-this.html).

faq.q: Does my dog really need a coat in winter?
faq.a: It depends on breed, coat thickness, size, age and temperature. Small dogs, short-haired breeds, seniors and dogs with health conditions feel the cold much sooner. Watch for slowing down, lifting paws, shivering or reluctance to continue — those are signs it is time to go in or put a coat on.

faq.q: How do I measure my dog for a coat?
faq.a: Measure from the base of the neck to the base of the tail for back length, and around the widest part of the chest just behind the front legs. Between sizes, size up for a broad or thick-coated dog and down for a lean one. You should fit two fingers between coat and body.

faq.q: Can I leave a dog coat on indoors?
faq.a: Not usually. A coat is for outdoor activity; leaving it on inside can cause overheating, and it stops you noticing when your dog is damp or rubbing. Take it off, dry it if needed, and let your dog's skin breathe.

posts.title: The lick sleeve I wish we had after our dog's surgery
posts.excerpt: After our dog's leg surgery, the cone came home with us and so did a week of quiet guilt. She could not eat properly — the plastic clattered into the bowl every
body: After our dog's leg surgery, the cone came home with us and so did a week of quiet guilt. She could not eat properly — the plastic clattered into the bowl every time she lowered her head. She could not drink without banging her nose on the rim. She spent most of the evening lying near us looking as though we had done it to her on purpose. The vet was right that she needed protection. The cone was just a miserable way to provide it.
## Why dogs lick a wound — and why you should stop it

Licking feels soothing to a dog. It is a grooming behaviour, and the repetitive motion genuinely calms them, which is why a dog will often lick a sore spot rather than rest. The problem is what the licking does to the wound. Saliva is not sterile, and a wound that stays wet does not heal cleanly. Repeated licking breaks down the delicate new tissue trying to form, keeps the area inflamed, and can turn a small incision into an infection that needs another round of antibiotics.

There is a second issue that catches people out. A dog who is allowed to lick a comfortable wound does not stop when it starts to hurt. They often lick harder, because the sensation is unusual, and by the time you notice raw skin around the incision you have a bigger problem than the one the surgery was meant to fix. Vets are firm about this for a reason, and it is worth taking seriously even when your dog looks perfectly content.
## What a lick sleeve does differently

A lick sleeve covers the area instead of blocking the whole head. That single change transforms the week. Your dog can eat from a bowl, drink normally, see where they are going, and sleep without a plastic ring propping their head up. For a leg wound, that is a massive quality-of-life difference in the first seven days, which is usually the hardest stretch.

The [Dog Anti-Lick Sleeve](/products/pth-1602.html) also has metal support bars built into the design. That matters because post-operative legs are rarely just a licking problem. There is usually an element of instability too — your dog is reluctant to put weight down, the joint wobbles, and they compensate with the rest of their body. The sleeve addresses both issues at once: it stops the tongue and gives the leg some structure while the area heals. Fewer problems to manage means a calmer house.

I should be clear about what it is not. This is not a magic recovery device, and it is not a substitute for the cone in every situation. A wound near the shoulder or the body may need a different approach, and your vet's advice always wins over anything written here. But for a lower-leg incision, a sleeve is worth asking about at the pre-op appointment rather than discovering afterwards.
## Fit is the part people get wrong

A sleeve that is too loose will slide down the leg, bunch above the joint, or get chewed straight through. One that is too tight can restrict circulation and rub the skin raw. Neither is obvious from a size label. Measure your dog's leg circumference at the widest point and check it against the size chart, then measure again a day or two after surgery, because swelling can change the fit considerably in the first forty-eight hours.

Check the sleeve twice a day at first — once in the morning and once after your dog has been moving around. Slip a finger underneath to make sure it is not pressing into the skin, and look for red marks or hair loss around the straps. Hair matting under the fabric is common, especially on long-coated dogs, so keep the area clean and dry. A little careful grooming around the edges prevents most of the problems people run into.

Some dogs try to remove a sleeve within minutes. Others ignore it completely. If yours spends the first hour shaking the leg, do not assume it is unbearable — give them a distraction, a chew toy that does not involve the operated leg, and a quiet room. Most settle once they realise it is not going anywhere. If they are genuinely distressed, pawing frantically or refusing to stand, take it off and call the vet rather than toughing it out.
## Living with a sleeve: the daily routine

The practical side is simpler than you might expect. Put the sleeve on in the morning, ideally before your dog has had a chance to reach the wound. Check it after meals, after any outdoor time, and before bed. Take it off for supervised rest periods if your vet recommends that, and always remove it for a proper skin check. Keep a spare if you can — a sleeve that gets wet or soiled needs to dry thoroughly before it goes back on, and having a second one avoids the awkward half-hour where your dog is uncovered.

Cleaning is straightforward. Most sleeves can be hand-washed in warm water with mild soap and air-dried flat. Do not put them in a hot tumble dryer; heat can damage the support bars and the fabric around them. If your dog goes outside while wearing it, wipe off mud before it dries into the material. Keeping it clean is not just about smell — a damp, dirty sleeve against healing skin is exactly the environment you are trying to avoid.

You will also need to manage activity. A dog in a sleeve often feels better than they actually are, and will try to resume normal life too early. Short, gentle walks on a lead, no jumping, no stairs if you can avoid them, and no unsupervised time with other dogs who might roughhouse. This is the unglamorous part of recovery, and it is where most setbacks happen.
## When to stop using it

Most dogs need a lick sleeve for one to two weeks, but the timeline comes from your vet, not from a product page. The signs that you can stop are usually a fully closed wound, no redness or discharge, and a dog who has stopped trying to reach the area. Do not extend the use indefinitely out of caution — a sleeve worn longer than necessary can cause its own skin irritation and muscle weakness from disuse.

When you do take it off for good, expect a day or two of extra interest in the leg. The sensation of air on healing skin is strange, and your dog may lick out of novelty. Supervise, offer a chew, and redirect. By the end of the second day it usually becomes boring again.
## The two mistakes I see most often

The first is taking the sleeve off too early because the dog seems fine. Dogs are excellent at appearing fine. A wound can look closed on the surface and still be fragile underneath, and a dog who has been comfortable for a day will happily go back to licking out of habit. Remove the sleeve only on your vet's timeline, not on your dog's apparent mood. If you are unsure, one more day is cheap insurance compared with a return visit.

The second mistake is the opposite: leaving it on longer than advised because you are nervous about removing it. A sleeve that stays on past the point of need causes its own problems — matted fur, skin irritation, and a leg that has been supported so long the muscles weaken. There is a window where the sleeve helps and a point where it starts to hinder. Your vet knows where that line is. When in doubt, make the call with them rather than alone, and do not let either anxiety or impatience make the decision for you.
## Preparing the house before surgery day

A little preparation makes the recovery week dramatically easier. Put a soft bed somewhere quiet but central, so your dog can rest without being isolated. Clear the route to the door of rugs and loose mats, because a dog on three legs slips easily. If you have stairs, decide in advance how you will carry your dog up and down — a large dog may need a sling and a second person. Keep food and water at a level they can reach without putting weight on the operated leg, and have a supply of the sleeve and cleaning materials in before the appointment rather than shopping for them afterwards.

It also helps to think about the other animals in the house. A dog returning from surgery smells different, and resident pets can react with excitement or suspicion. Keep introductions calm and supervised for the first day or two, and do not let other dogs nose at the sleeve or the wound. Feeding separately avoids the tension that can build up around a bowl when one dog cannot move quickly. A quiet, predictable household is the best thing you can offer a dog whose body is doing repair work, and it costs nothing but a little planning.

If you are facing a post-op week at home, ask your vet about a sleeve before you leave the clinic. It made our house quieter, it let our dog eat like a normal dog, and it removed the worst part of the cone experience. Recovery is slow enough without making it uncomfortable.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [A pet travel backpack that doesn't turn every outing into a workout](/blog/pet-travel-backpack-that-doesnt-hurt.html), [What to ask a pet supplies distributor before your first order](/blog/what-to-ask-a-pet-supplies-distributor.html), [My cat hated carriers until we tried a clear one](/blog/my-cat-hated-carriers-until-a-clear-one.html).

faq.q: Can my dog wear a lick sleeve instead of a cone?
faq.a: For many leg wounds, yes — ask your vet. A sleeve protects the site without blocking vision or eating, which most dogs tolerate far better. It is not suitable for every wound location, particularly around the face, flank or tail.

faq.q: How long can a dog wear a lick sleeve?
faq.a: Usually one to two weeks during healing. Remove it daily to check the skin, keep it clean and dry, and stop using it if you notice swelling, rubbing or an unpleasant smell. Your vet's timeline takes priority.

faq.q: Can my dog walk in a lick sleeve?
faq.a: Short, gentle lead walks are usually fine and often encouraged, but check with your vet first. Avoid running, jumping, stairs and rough play until the wound has closed and your vet clears normal activity.

posts.title: What a blind dog halo actually does (and what it can't)
posts.excerpt: The first time I saw a blind dog wearing a halo, I thought it looked strange — a soft padded ring around the head, like a tiny bumper car. Then I watched the do
body: The first time I saw a blind dog wearing a halo, I thought it looked strange — a soft padded ring around the head, like a tiny bumper car. Then I watched the dog walk across a room without hesitating, bump the ring gently against a table corner, turn their head slightly, and carry on. No flinch, no yelp, no confusion. It made sense immediately. What looked odd was actually a piece of equipment that let a dog keep being a dog.
## The problem it solves is simple

Dogs who lose their sight do not lose their confidence or their desire to explore. They still want to move around the house, find their people, and do all the things they did before. What they lose is the ability to judge where solid objects are. A halo gives them a physical signal before their head hits something hard. It is not a guide and it does not replace training — it is a warning system they can feel, arriving a fraction of a second before contact.

That fraction matters more than it sounds. A blind dog moving confidently through a familiar room can still misjudge a chair that was moved thirty centimetres, or a person who left a bag on the floor. A knocked head is painful and, more importantly, it makes a dog hesitant. After a few bumps, some dogs start refusing to move around without guidance. Preventing those bumps is about protecting confidence as much as protecting skin.
## How blind dogs actually navigate

It helps to understand what your dog is doing before you buy anything. Blind dogs navigate mainly by memory and smell. They build a mental map of the house — where the sofa ends, how many steps to the water bowl, which way the hallway turns — and they use scent and sound to confirm it. This is why moving furniture is genuinely disruptive, and why most blind dogs do better when the layout stays predictable.

They also use whiskers and the air pressure changes near walls and objects, but those senses have limits. A thin table leg or an open cabinet door at head height can be invisible to all of them until contact. A halo extends the range at which a dog detects a boundary, giving them time to stop or turn. Used alongside a consistent home layout, it fills in the gaps that memory and smell cannot cover.

This is also why a halo is more useful indoors than outdoors. Inside, the obstacles are fixed and repeatable, and the dog learns to work around them. Outside, everything moves — people, bikes, other dogs — and no ring can make a busy pavement safe. A halo is a tool for the environment you control.
## Why a harness matters more than the ring

The ring is the visible part, so it gets all the attention. The harness is what makes it usable. A halo that slips, spins around the head, or rides up over the eyes is worse than useless, because it interferes with hearing and smell while failing to protect anything. You want a setup that sits steady, stays clear of the ears, and can be put on without a daily struggle.

Look at how the ring attaches. A rigid connection that transmits every knock straight to the dog's skull is not ideal; a little give absorbs the impact and turns it into a soft signal. Check the padding around the head too, because this is equipment your dog will wear for hours at a time. Seams in the wrong place will rub behind the ears within a week. Our [Blind Dog Halo Harness](/products/pth-1604.html) keeps the ring stable on a lightweight frame while leaving the ears and nose unobstructed — the goal is protection your dog stops noticing.

The harness should also have an adjustment range that suits your dog's head and chest. A halo that fits a collie will not fit a terrier, and a 'one size' claim usually means it fits neither well. Measure around the head just behind the ears and around the chest, and check the sizing before you order.
## What it cannot do

I want to be blunt about the limits, because disappointment here is avoidable. A halo will not make your dog navigate a new house overnight. It will not stop them stepping off a stair, into a pool, or under a low gate, because the ring sits around the head and does not protect the feet or body. It will not replace supervision in the first weeks after vision loss, and it will not stop a determined dog from squeezing somewhere they should not.

It also will not fix the emotional side of losing sight. Some dogs become anxious, some become clingy, some withdraw. A halo helps them move safely, which supports confidence, but the adjustment is gradual and it involves you — your voice, your routine, your patience. Think of it as one part of a broader approach rather than a solution on its own.

If someone tells you a halo makes a blind dog see again, or that it removes the need to supervise, they are selling something. What it really does is reduce the number of painful bumps while your dog learns or relearns the layout. That is a modest claim. It is also a genuinely useful one, and for many owners it is the difference between a dog who moves freely and a dog who waits to be led.
## Setting up your home

The halo works best in a home that is set up for a blind dog. Keep furniture in the same place. Put a textured mat at the top and bottom of stairs so your dog can feel the change in surface. Use a bell or a verbal cue before you approach, so you never startle them. Block off hazards consistently rather than sometimes — a gate that is sometimes closed teaches nothing.

You can also use scent to mark important places. A tiny amount of a consistent, safe scent near the water bowl or the bed gives your dog a landmark they can navigate by. Avoid changing it frequently. The whole system depends on things staying the same, and the halo simply gives your dog a little more forgiveness when something inevitably does change.

Introduce discomfort slowly. Some dogs accept a halo in minutes. Others need several days of wearing it indoors for short periods while you sit nearby with treats. Do not force it on for a full day straight away, and do not put it on and immediately leave the room. Let them associate it with calm, pleasant company, then gradually extend the time as it becomes familiar.
## Give it a trial period

Watch your dog's body language for the first week. Ears back, head shaking, and trying to rub the halo off are signs to reassess the fit or the introduction, not necessarily to abandon the idea. A dog who walks normally, eats normally, and stops reacting to it after a day or two has accepted it. Some never do, and that is fine too — every dog adapts differently, and a halo is optional equipment, not a requirement.
## Noticing the loss early makes everything easier

Vision loss rarely happens all at once. Many dogs go gradually blind, and owners often miss the early signs because the dog compensates so well. They start bumping into furniture in dim light, hesitate before jumping onto the sofa, or seem startled when you approach from one side. Their eyes may look cloudy or cloudy in one eye only. If you notice any of this, a vet visit is worth it — some causes are treatable, and even when they are not, knowing what is happening lets you adapt the home before your dog starts losing confidence.

The adjustment is easier for everyone when it starts calmly. Keep the furniture where it is, keep the food and water bowls in the same spot, and use your voice before you touch your dog. Add a verbal marker for important places — 'bed', 'water', 'outside' — and use the same words every time. Dogs who lose their sight often rely more heavily on their hearing, and a consistent vocabulary becomes a map. A halo fits into this picture as one piece of equipment among several, not as the answer to the whole problem.

Exercise needs a rethink too. A blind dog can still enjoy a good walk, but the environment has to be predictable. Use a familiar route, keep the same lead, and avoid off-lead time in places you have not walked before. A long line gives more freedom while still keeping your dog within reach, and it lets you steer them away from hazards before they bump into them. Many owners find their dog becomes more confident outdoors once they have a reliable routine, and the halo is useful on the sections where the path narrows or furniture-like obstacles appear.

If you are looking for the best blind dog halo, judge it on fit, stability, padding and how little it interferes with hearing and smell. Ignore the photos of dogs looking heroic in bright colours. The right one disappears into your dog's routine, and one day you notice they crossed the room and bumped nothing at all.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [Living with a torn ACL: what a leg brace can and can't do](/blog/living-with-a-torn-acl-what-a-brace-can-do.html), ['Airline approved' is not a stamp — here's what to check](/blog/airline-approved-is-not-a-stamp.html), [A waterproof dog coat is really about the walk after the rain stops](/blog/waterproof-dog-coat-is-about-the-walk-after.html).

faq.q: Do blind dogs really benefit from a halo?
faq.a: Many do. A halo reduces head bumps against furniture and walls, which helps a blind dog move more confidently. It works best alongside a consistent home layout and scent or verbal cues, not as a standalone solution.

faq.q: How do I introduce a halo to my blind dog?
faq.a: Let them sniff it first, then put it on for short periods indoors while giving treats or praise. Keep sessions calm and positive, stay nearby, and gradually extend the time as they stop trying to rub it off.

faq.q: Can a blind dog wear a halo all day?
faq.a: Many dogs do, but start gradually and check the skin and padding daily for rubbing. Take it off if it interferes with eating, drinking or hearing, and recheck the fit as your dog adjusts.

posts.title: 'Airline approved' is not a stamp — here's what to check
posts.excerpt: I once watched a family get stopped at check-in because their carrier was two centimetres too tall. The bag had 'airline approved' printed on the tag in large l
body: I once watched a family get stopped at check-in because their carrier was two centimetres too tall. The bag had 'airline approved' printed on the tag in large letters. The airline disagreed. There was a quiet, awkward rearrangement of luggage in the middle of the terminal while their dog watched from inside the carrier, wondering what was happening. They eventually got through, but the first hour of their holiday was spent apologising to other passengers. I have never forgotten it.
## There is no universal approval

That phrase on a product page is marketing shorthand, not an official certification. There is no global authority that stamps carriers as approved. Every airline sets its own under-seat dimensions, and those dimensions vary by aircraft — the same airline can have different limits on a short-haul regional jet and a long-haul widebody. The number printed on a bag is usually a best guess at what most airlines accept most of the time.

Your job is to check the airline you are actually flying with, on the day you book, and again a week before departure. Find the pet policy page, note the maximum height, width and depth for in-cabin carriers, and write them down. Policies change with aircraft rotations, and a friendly phone call to customer service is worth more than a hundred reviews. If the airline will not give you a clear answer, assume the smaller dimension and plan around it.

The phrase 'airline approved' is still useful as a rough signal — it usually means the bag is in the right general size range and has enough ventilation. Just treat it as a starting point, not a promise. The two centimetres in that story were the whole problem.
## Measure the bag, not the box

The most common mistake is measuring the packaging or trusting the product description instead of the object. Take a tape measure to the actual carrier. Measure the outside, at the widest points, including wheels, handles, feet, and any protruding clips. Soft carriers can be squashed a little to fit under a seat; hard-sided ones cannot. If you fly often, that distinction decides which bag you should own.

Then add a margin. A carrier that exactly matches the published limit is a carrier that will fail if the measurement was taken slightly differently at the gate. Two centimetres of slack has saved more trips than any feature I can think of. If your pet's comfort allows it, choose a bag comfortably under the limit rather than one that pushes right up to it.

You also need to check the weight rule. Some airlines include the pet and carrier in your hand luggage allowance; others do not. A hard shell is heavier before anything goes inside, and on a strict airline that extra kilo matters. Weigh the packed carrier at home, with your pet inside if they will tolerate it for a minute, and know the number before you leave for the airport.
## Hard shell or soft sided

This is the decision people agonise over, and it really comes down to how you travel. A soft-sided carrier is lighter, flexes to fit awkward spaces, and is easier to stow under a seat. It is also easier for a determined animal to damage, and it offers less protection if a bag gets dropped or stacked on. For a calm, small pet on occasional flights, soft sides are usually the practical choice.

A hard shell gives better protection and holds its shape, which matters on long journeys and when your carrier is handled by other people. It is easier to clean after an accident, and the structure makes a nervous dog feel less exposed. The trade-offs are weight and zero flexibility — if it is too tall, no amount of pushing will make it fit. Our [Hard-Sided Pet Carrier](/products/pth-1106.html) uses a PP and ABS shell in three two-tone colourways, built for people who fly enough to care about what happens to the bag between check-in and arrival.

There is a middle ground in carriers with a rigid base and a flexible top, but they are not ideal for every airline. Whichever you choose, remember that airlines sometimes require the animal to be visible or reachable. A fully enclosed hard case with tiny windows can cause problems on check-in even when the dimensions are perfect, so check the airline's rules about ventilation openings before you commit.
## The details that survive a real trip

Look at the latches, the handle attachment, and the door. These are the parts that break, and they are the parts nobody photographs. A door that can pop open under pressure is a genuine emergency at thirty thousand feet. Two secure latches, a door that locks positively, and a handle anchored into the shell rather than glued onto it are worth more than a dozen pockets.

Ventilation needs the same scrutiny. Air circulates differently under a seat than it does in a cabin, and a carrier with holes on only one side can leave your pet in a pocket of stale air. Check that there are openings on at least two opposing sides, and that the pet can see out. A dog who can watch the cabin is generally calmer than one who cannot. Slide the carrier partway under the seat before you board and see whether the openings remain uncovered once it is in position — this is a common oversight.

The interior is worth thinking about too. Put down an absorbent pad rather than a loose towel that can bunch up, and bring a familiar-smelling item from home. Freeze a small water bottle the night before so it thaws slowly during the flight, and attach it securely so it does not roll around. None of this affects whether the carrier is approved, but all of it affects whether your pet arrives relaxed.
## The day of the flight

Get to the airport early. Not the usual early — genuinely early. Check-in staff deal with pet travel inconsistently, and the extra time lets you sort out a problem without watching the gate close. Have the carrier, the booking reference, any health documents, and the airline's pet policy printed or saved on your phone. Do not rely on the agent knowing the rules by heart.

At security, you will usually need to take your pet out of the carrier. Practise this at home so it is not a wrestling match in front of a queue. A harness and a short lead make it much easier to keep hold of an animal who would rather bolt. Put the lead on before you open the carrier door, every time, without exception. The number of pets lost at airports because someone opened a door first is far higher than people realise.

During the flight, keep the carrier under the seat in front rather than at your feet if the rules allow. It is more stable there and less likely to be kicked. Speak to your pet quietly at intervals, and do not open the door in the cabin — a scared animal in a pressurized aircraft is a nightmare to recapture. If you need to check on them, use a phone camera angled into the carrier rather than unzipping it.
## Do a rehearsal

Before the real flight, take your carrier to a cinema, a train, or a friend's house. See if it fits under a seat. See how your pet behaves in it for two hours. See how you manage carrying it while also holding a passport, a boarding pass, and a coffee. The cheapest mistakes to fix are the ones you make at home, and the rehearsal turns a list of worries into a short list of things you still need to sort out.
## If flying is not the right choice

It is worth saying that flying with a pet is not always the kindest option, whatever carrier you buy. For a short journey, a car or train can be calmer, more predictable, and far less stressful for an animal who dislikes noise and unfamiliar handling. If you are moving house with a dog and the drive is a day, the drive may genuinely be the better choice. A carrier still matters on that journey — a secured crate or a well-fitted seat belt harness keeps everyone safe — but the pressure to find the perfect airline carrier disappears.

When flying is unavoidable, book direct flights wherever possible. Each connection is another security line, another gate change, and another chance for a well-meaning member of staff to misapply the rules. Tell the airline at booking that you are travelling with a pet in the cabin, and again at check-in. Bring printed copies of the policy. Being politely persistent with documentation has got more pets onto flights than any argument about the word 'approved' printed on a bag.

An airline approved pet carrier is really just a carrier you have checked carefully. Do the measuring yourself, check the specific airline, read the policy, and leave a margin. Then the phrase on the tag stops mattering, because you already know it will fit.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [The lick sleeve I wish we had after our dog's surgery](/blog/the-lick-sleeve-i-wish-we-had-after-surgery.html), [Why I stopped holding the leash on morning runs](/blog/why-i-stopped-holding-the-leash-on-runs.html), [Looking at a Carhartt dog jacket? Here's what to compare before you buy](/blog/looking-at-a-carhartt-dog-jacket-compare-this.html).

faq.q: What size carrier fits under an airplane seat?
faq.a: It varies by airline and aircraft, but a common limit is around 40 x 30 x 20 cm. Always check your airline's published pet policy before booking, and measure the outside of the carrier including wheels, handles and clips.

faq.q: Can my dog fly in a hard-sided carrier?
faq.a: Yes, if it fits the airline's size rules and your dog can stand, turn around and lie down comfortably. Confirm the airline allows rigid carriers in the cabin — a few only accept soft-sided bags.

faq.q: What should I put in a carrier for a flight?
faq.a: An absorbent pad, a familiar-smelling blanket or t-shirt, and a water source that will not spill — a frozen bottle works well. Avoid loose toys that can roll around, and attach a lead to your pet before opening the carrier at security.

posts.title: My cat hated carriers until we tried a clear one
posts.excerpt: My cat's relationship with carriers was simple: she refused. The moment a box came out of the cupboard, she vanished — under the bed, behind the sofa, anywhere
body: My cat's relationship with carriers was simple: she refused. The moment a box came out of the cupboard, she vanished — under the bed, behind the sofa, anywhere with a roof and a gap. I tried treats. I tried leaving it open for days. I tried a hooded backpack that I thought looked friendly and cosy. Nothing. Then a friend suggested a clear one, and the difference was almost immediate. Within a week she was walking into it on her own.
## Why visibility changes everything

A cat in a dark, enclosed carrier is a cat who cannot see what is happening to them. That is frightening in a way humans tend to underestimate. We rely on sight to make sense of movement; take it away and every sound becomes a threat with no explanation. A clear panel lets your cat watch the world, and watching gives them a measure of control. For an anxious cat, seeing out is often far calmer than being hidden away.

There is a flip side, and I should mention it honestly. Some cats feel exposed in a clear carrier and prefer the security of a covered one. If your cat is bold and curious, visibility is likely to help. If they are the type who hide from guests for hours, you may need to compromise — a clear front with a partially covered back and sides can give both reassurance and a view. Watch what your cat does rather than assuming the feature works for all animals.
## Clear does not mean flimsy

The transparent part needs to be tough, and the bag still needs airflow. Look at where the ventilation holes sit in relation to the clear window. Holes only at the top are not enough — a cat's body heat builds up around them, and fresh air needs to move across the whole space. The [Transparent Pet Backpack](/products/pth-1104.html) has the clear window set into a body with ventilation around it, so the view does not come at the cost of airflow.

Check the material too. A window that scratches easily will cloud over after a handful of trips, and then you have paid extra for a feature that no longer works. Scratch-resistant clear panels cost more to manufacture but stay usable for years. Press on the window when you are inspecting a bag — if it flexes a lot, it is more likely to crack at the edges over time. The seams around the clear section are another weak point, since fabric and plastic expand at different rates in heat.

It comes in four colours, which matters less than people think, but there is one practical consideration. A dark frame around a clear window makes it easier for your cat to see out, because the contrast helps them focus on the view. A very light frame can make the window look like a bright, confusing hole from the inside. Minor detail, but it is the kind of thing your cat notices and you do not.
## Introduce it as furniture, not transport

My biggest mistake with every previous carrier was bringing it out only when we were leaving the house. Your cat learns that pattern fast. Bag appears, something frightening follows. By the time you need the carrier, the object itself is a signal that makes them run. You have to rewrite that association before the vet appointment, not during it.

Leave the backpack open in the living room, in a spot your cat already uses. Put an old t-shirt of yours inside — unwashed is fine, better even, because your smell is familiar and calming. Feed near it for a couple of days, then just inside the opening, then further in. Move slowly enough that your cat never feels trapped. If they are eating comfortably inside with the door open, you are making progress.

Only after several days should you zip it, and then only for a few seconds at first. Zip, treat, unzip. Repeat until the zip becomes boring. Then try lifting the bag an inch off the floor while they are inside. Then carrying it to the next room. Each step is tiny, and each step matters more than the last one. Rushing the sequence is how you end up with a cat who panics at the sight of a backpack.
## A step-by-step desensitisation that works

Here is the routine I eventually landed on, and it took about ten days. Days one to three: backpack open in the room, treats near and then inside. Days four and five: meals served just inside the opening. Days six and seven: zip for five seconds while your cat is eating, then unzip before they finish. Days eight and nine: zip and lift, zip and walk two steps, always with a treat at the end. Day ten: a short trip to the car and back, no engine, no vet, just a return to the house with a reward.

The key is that nothing bad ever happens immediately after the backpack. No car journey to the clinic, no stranger poking at them, no forced exit. If you need to go to the vet, use a different carrier for the first few trips if you have one, and keep the backpack associated with pleasant, boring outcomes. Once the association is solid, you can use it for everything.

Expect setbacks. A cat who was fine with the bag yesterday may refuse today, especially after a stressful event. Go back one step for a day and move forward again. This is normal, not failure. The whole process is about building a history of the backpack predicting neutral or good things, and history takes time to accumulate.
## When a backpack is not the answer

A cat carrier backpack is excellent for short journeys, vet visits, and moving through places where you need your hands free. It is not ideal for every situation. A cat who is very heavy will make a backpack uncomfortable to wear for more than twenty minutes. A cat who panics at being enclosed may do better in a rigid carrier with a door they can see through. And for long journeys, a carrier that can sit on the floor and be covered with a towel is usually less stressful than one strapped to your back.

There is also a practical limit on air travel. Many airlines accept a soft backpack under the seat, but the dimensions need checking, and a backpack that bulges at the top may be refused even if it fits on paper. If you fly regularly with your cat, a more structured carrier might be the safer investment, even if the backpack is better for everyday use.

I still use ours constantly — for the short walk to the car, for the vet, for moving house. But I stopped treating it as the one perfect solution. It is one tool among several, and knowing when to leave it at home is part of using it well.
## Cleaning and keeping it fresh

Cats are sensitive to smell, and a carrier that smells of a previous stressful trip can undo your careful training. Wipe the interior down after each use with a damp cloth and a mild, unscented cleaner. Avoid anything with a strong fragrance — what smells fresh to you is overwhelming to a cat. Let the bag air out fully before you put it away, and store it somewhere that does not smell of cleaning products.

Check the zips and the clear panel regularly. A zip that catches can pinch your cat, and a scratched window defeats the entire reason you bought a clear backpack. Keep the bag out of direct sunlight when stored, since prolonged UV exposure can make clear panels cloudy over time. These are small habits, but they keep the bag in the condition that made your cat accept it in the first place.
## Reading your cat's signals

The whole process depends on noticing when your cat is relaxed and when they are merely tolerating things. Ears slightly forward, a loose tail, and eating normally are good signs. Flattened ears, a twitching tail, dilated pupils and a tense body mean you have pushed too far. The moment you see those signals, go back a step. A cat who is stressed in a carrier will remember it, and the next session starts from a worse place than the last one.

This is why I never combined the backpack with anything genuinely unpleasant during training. If a vet visit was due, I used a different carrier for the first few trips and kept the backpack for short, boring journeys. It sounds overly careful until you have spent three weeks rebuilding trust that took thirty seconds to break. Cats are patient animals, but they are also precise about cause and effect. Give them a clear, consistent story about the backpack and they will eventually write themselves into it.

If you are shopping for a cat carrier backpack and your cat is the cautious type, try a clear one. It is the closest thing to letting them come with you without feeling trapped — provided you give them the time to discover that for themselves.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [Living with a torn ACL: what a leg brace can and can't do](/blog/living-with-a-torn-acl-what-a-brace-can-do.html), [What a blind dog halo actually does (and what it can't)](/blog/what-a-blind-dog-halo-actually-does.html), [A waterproof dog coat is really about the walk after the rain stops](/blog/waterproof-dog-coat-is-about-the-walk-after.html).

faq.q: Do cats prefer clear carriers?
faq.a: Many anxious cats do, because they can see their surroundings instead of sitting in the dark. It is not universal — some cats feel exposed — but for a cat who panics in a covered carrier, a clear panel is often worth trying.

faq.q: How do I get my cat into a carrier without a fight?
faq.a: Turn the carrier into ordinary furniture first. Leave it open with familiar bedding, feed near and then inside it, and only zip it for a few seconds at a time once your cat goes in voluntarily. Build up over days, never force the first trip, and keep the carrier associated with calm outcomes.

faq.q: Is a cat backpack comfortable to wear for long walks?
faq.a: For short trips, yes. For longer walks, check the strap padding and back support, keep the bag close to your body, and plan breaks with water. If your cat is heavy or the walk is more than half an hour, a trolley carrier may be kinder to your back.

posts.title: Living with a torn ACL: what a leg brace can and can't do
posts.excerpt: The vet said the word 'surgery' and my dog responded by refusing to put weight on her back leg. I am fairly sure she understood the tone even if she did not und
body: The vet said the word 'surgery' and my dog responded by refusing to put weight on her back leg. I am fairly sure she understood the tone even if she did not understand the word. A torn ACL is common in active dogs, and the decision ahead of you is rarely simple. It involves money, your dog's age, their size, how much activity they need, and a lot of uncomfortable guessing. A brace is part of that conversation — but it is not a replacement for it.
## Understanding the injury

The cranial cruciate ligament — the dog equivalent of the ACL — stabilises the knee and stops the lower leg from sliding forward relative to the upper leg. When it tears, the joint becomes unstable. Your dog may hold the leg up, toe-touch it, or walk with a stiff, shortened stride. Some tears happen suddenly during a run or a twist; others develop slowly over months as the ligament degenerates.

The knee is not a simple hinge. It rotates slightly and absorbs twist, which is exactly what makes it vulnerable. Unlike a torn ligament in a human knee, a complete cruciate tear in a dog does not usually heal on its own, because the joint keeps moving and the torn ends never get the chance to reconnect. That is why vets talk about surgery so readily. The question for most owners is not whether the joint is stable — it is not — but what to do about it.
## What a brace actually does

A knee brace does not repair a torn ligament. I want to say that plainly, because the phrase 'support' gets interpreted as 'heals' far too often. What a brace does is stabilise the joint so your dog can move with less wobble and less pain while the area heals, while you make a decision, or as a long-term management tool if surgery is not on the table.

Think of it as external support for a joint that has lost its internal support. By limiting the unwanted motion, a brace reduces the repeated stress on the meniscus and the joint surfaces. For some dogs, especially smaller ones or those with partial tears, that is enough to restore comfortable movement. For others it buys time — time to save for surgery, time to get a second opinion, or time to see whether conservative management works.
## The support bar is the point

A soft neoprene sleeve alone will not stabilise a knee. It provides warmth and mild compression, which feels nice, but it cannot stop the tibia from shifting. You need something rigid enough to resist that motion. The [Dog Leg Brace](/products/pth-1603.html) has a metal support bar built into the hind-leg design, along with straps that hold the brace in place as your dog walks. That combination matters.

Rotation is the failure mode of most braces. A dog walks, the muscle changes shape, the brace twists a few degrees, and suddenly the support bar is on the side of the knee instead of the front. Once that happens, the brace is doing nothing except rubbing. Good strapping above and below the joint keeps the bar aligned through the whole stride. When you fit a brace, check that the bar sits over the front of the knee and stays there after your dog has walked twenty metres.

The other thing to look for is how the brace handles the hock and the foot. A hind-leg brace that extends too far down can interfere with the way your dog pushes off, which makes them compensate and can create problems in the opposite leg. The aim is enough structure to stabilise the knee, and no more.
## Fit and skin checks are not optional

A brace that is too tight will rub and can cause sores; one that is too loose will slide and fail to support anything. Measure around the leg above and below the knee, follow the size chart, and check the fit while your dog is standing rather than lying down. Legs change shape when weight is on them. If you are between sizes, ask the supplier rather than guessing — a half-size mistake is the difference between a useful brace and an expensive paperweight.

Check the skin under the brace every day at first. Look for red marks, hair loss, or a sore spot where a strap crosses. Keep the area clean and dry, and take the brace off for supervised rest periods as your vet advises. Dogs are remarkably good at hiding discomfort, so do not wait for whining. Watch how they move when the brace is off — if they are suddenly more willing to bear weight, the brace may have been causing a problem rather than solving one.

Build up wearing time gradually. Start with an hour or two indoors, check the skin, and extend from there. A dog who spends all day in a brace from day one is much more likely to develop rubbing or to resent the whole experience. Keep the brace clean too — a damp, dirty brace against healing skin is an avoidable problem.
## The rehabilitation timeline

Recovery is measured in weeks, not days, and the first two are usually the hardest. During that time the goal is simple: reduce inflammation, protect the joint, and stop your dog from doing anything that makes it worse. Strict rest is boring for everyone involved, but it is the foundation. Short, slow lead walks for toilet breaks, no stairs, no jumping, and no off-lead time in the park.

After the initial period, controlled movement becomes important. Muscles that are not used will waste, and a weak leg puts more stress on the joint. Your vet may suggest specific exercises — slow walking on a flat surface, sitting and standing, gradual incline work. These should be done consistently and gently. More is not better at this stage; a little every day beats a long session once a week.

Weight management matters more than most owners expect. Every extra kilo adds load to an unstable joint, and even modest weight loss can make a noticeable difference to how your dog moves. If your vet recommends a target weight, take it seriously. This is one of the few parts of recovery entirely within your control.
## Working with your vet

A brace without a plan is just equipment. Ask your vet specific questions: Is the tear complete or partial? Is the meniscus involved? Would surgery be appropriate given my dog's age and size? What does conservative management realistically look like over six months? What are the signs that the brace approach is failing? The answers shape everything else, and a good vet will welcome the questions.

If surgery is recommended, a brace can still be useful before and after. Before, it can make your dog more comfortable while you prepare. After, it may be part of the rehabilitation protocol, though the timing must come from your surgeon. Do not assume that a brace means you can skip the surgical conversation — and do not assume that surgery means a brace is pointless. They are tools that can work together.

Get a second opinion if the decision feels too big to make alone. A different vet may offer a different approach, and hearing the same recommendation twice is reassuring in its own way. What you want is a plan you understand and can actually follow for the next few months.
## Keeping a record that helps

Recovery is slow enough that it is easy to lose track of whether things are improving. I started taking a short video every few days — same room, same surface, same time of day. Watching them side by side showed a gradual improvement I could not see day to day, and that was genuinely encouraging during the flat weeks. It also gave the vet something concrete to look at instead of relying on my description of 'a bit better'.

Write down the dates too: when the brace arrived, when you first used it, when you extended the wearing time, when you noticed any rubbing. If a problem arises, that record turns a confusing situation into a clear one. Keep a note of weight as well, since even a small change affects the load on the joint. None of this takes more than a minute, and it gives you something to hold on to when progress feels invisible.

The other thing worth planning is your own routine around the dog's limits. Recovery rarely fits neatly around a normal working week, so decide in advance who handles the short walks, who does the evening skin check, and what happens on the days you are out. A dog in recovery thrives on predictability, and a shared plan between the people in the house matters as much as any piece of equipment. If you live alone, line up a friend or a neighbour for the days when you cannot be home at lunchtime. It is easier to arrange that now than to improvise it during a busy week.

We went the conservative route with our dog and managed well for a long time. That is not everyone's outcome, and I would not pretend our experience is a recommendation for yours. What a good brace gave us was time and a dog who could still enjoy short walks while we worked out the next step. If that is what you need too, talk to your vet about whether a hind-leg brace belongs in your plan.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.
## Keep reading

If you want to go deeper, these guides cover the same ground from a different angle: [The lick sleeve I wish we had after our dog's surgery](/blog/the-lick-sleeve-i-wish-we-had-after-surgery.html), [Why I stopped holding the leash on morning runs](/blog/why-i-stopped-holding-the-leash-on-runs.html), [Looking at a Carhartt dog jacket? Here's what to compare before you buy](/blog/looking-at-a-carhartt-dog-jacket-compare-this.html).

faq.q: Can a brace heal a torn ACL without surgery?
faq.a: A brace cannot repair the ligament, but it can stabilise the joint and improve comfort. Some dogs, especially smaller or less active ones, manage well with a brace, rest and weight control. Discuss the realistic options with your vet.

faq.q: How long does my dog need to wear a leg brace?
faq.a: It varies. Some dogs wear one during recovery, others long-term for joint stability. Start with short supervised periods, build up gradually, and check the skin daily for rubbing or irritation.

faq.q: Can my dog exercise in a leg brace?
faq.a: Gentle, controlled lead walks are usually part of rehabilitation, but running, jumping and off-lead play are out while the joint heals. Confirm an exercise plan with your vet and increase activity only as advised.

posts.title: What to ask a pet supplies distributor before your first order
posts.excerpt: The first wholesale order is the one that teaches you the most, usually by costing you something. I made the expensive version of this mistake — ordering a mixe
body: The first wholesale order is the one that teaches you the most, usually by costing you something. I made the expensive version of this mistake — ordering a mixed container straight from a catalogue without asking the questions that mattered. The products were fine. The assumptions were not. I had assumed minimums were flexible, that samples would be credited, and that the person who answered the first email would still be answering six months later. Two of those three were wrong.
## Start with the product, not the price list

A good distributor can tell you what a product is made of, what sizes it comes in, who it is for, and what the packaging looks like. If every answer is 'best quality' with no detail behind it, keep asking. Ask for the fabric, the hardware, the net weight, the folded size, the colours in stock. These specifics tell you whether the person on the other end knows the range or is simply forwarding a spreadsheet they did not write.

Ask which products are actually in stock versus made to order. That distinction affects your lead time more than anything else, and it is often glossed over in the first conversation. A supplier who says everything is available needs to back that up with a realistic production windows. If a company claims three-day delivery on custom colours, be sceptical until you see it in writing.

Then look at consistency. If the catalogue shows twelve models but the website only details six, ask about the other six. Gaps in a range usually mean something — discontinued lines, unreliable supply, or products the supplier does not actually hold. None of these are dealbreakers, but you want to know before you build a range around them.
## Ask about minimums in plain numbers

Minimum order quantities are where new buyers get trapped. Ask the MOQ per item and the MOQ per order, in actual units. Then ask whether you can mix models within one shipment. A supplier who can put twelve carriers, twenty leashes and ten coats into one order is very different from one who wants five hundred of a single SKU. If you are testing a market, flexibility at the start is worth more than a slightly better unit price.

Ask what happens when a size or colour sells out. Can you reorder that one item quickly, or do you have to place another full minimum? How long does a reorder take? These questions feel tedious on a first call and become urgent when your best-selling size runs out in the middle of a season.

Packaging minimums are worth checking too. Some suppliers will only produce custom packaging at high volumes, which means your first order ships in neutral bags. That is fine if you know it in advance and terrible if you were planning a branded launch. Ask early and build it into your budget.
## Samples are a conversation, not a favour

Always ask for samples before a bulk order, and ask plainly who pays. Many suppliers send samples free and charge only shipping; some credit the sample cost against your first order; a few charge full price and refund it later. All of these are normal. What is not normal is a refusal to let you touch the product before ordering hundreds of units.

When the samples arrive, check them properly. Look at the stitching at stress points, run the zips, test the clips, and smell the fabric. Check that the colours match the catalogue, because they often do not — screens lie and dye lots vary. Measure the sample against the stated dimensions. If the measurements are wrong on a sample, imagine what they will be like in a production run.

Give the sample to someone else to look at too. A fresh pair of eyes catches things you stop noticing after handling the same bag for ten minutes. And keep the samples. They are your reference when the bulk order arrives, and the only reliable way to answer the question 'is this what we agreed on?'
## Ask who you actually deal with

Will you have one contact or a different person each time? What hours do they work, and in which time zone? What happens when a shipment is delayed — who tells you, and how quickly? How are defective units handled? These questions feel awkward on a first call and become very important on the third order, when something has inevitably gone slightly wrong.

A supplier with a single point of contact is easier to work with, but check whether that person can actually make decisions or has to refer everything upward. Ask who signs off on a credit or a replacement. If nobody can give you a straight answer, you will discover the answer during a dispute, which is the worst possible time.

Communication style tells you a lot. A distributor who replies within a day, answers in full sentences, and admits when they do not know something is usually reliable. One who sends one-word replies, disappears for a week, or promises everything without checking is showing you how future problems will be handled.
## Shipping, duties and the fine print

Ask who arranges shipping and who pays for it, and get the incoterm in writing. FOB, EXW and CIF mean very different things in practice, and the price per unit is meaningless until you know what is included. Ask for a full landed-cost estimate to your door, including freight, insurance, duties and local delivery. A cheaper unit price can disappear fast once freight is added.

Find out how the goods are packed. Carton size and weight per carton affect your shipping cost directly, and products that fold flat can save a remarkable amount of space. Ask how many units fit in a carton and what the carton dimensions are. If your supplier cannot answer, ask them to send a photo of a packed carton.

Then ask about documents. You will need a commercial invoice, a packing list, and possibly certificates depending on your market and the materials involved. A distributor who has shipped to your country before will know exactly what is required. One who has not may learn at your expense, so ask for a reference from a customer in your region.
## Quality control and what happens when it goes wrong

Ask whether the supplier inspects goods before shipping, and whether you can request photos or a report before payment. Some will send a pre-shipment inspection with measurements and images. That is a good sign. If they say defects never happen, that is a less good sign — experienced suppliers know they do and have a process for catching them.

Get the complaint process in writing. What is the window for reporting a defect after delivery? Who pays for replacements? Do you return the faulty item or is it credited against the next order? What counts as a defect versus normal variation in a handmade product? A clear answer here protects both sides, and a vague one will be interpreted in the supplier's favour when it matters.

At Poteho we make a point of answering these questions early. Our [full range](/products.html) covers carriers, leashes, apparel, beds, fences and rehabilitation products, and we would rather explain the details now than fix a misunderstanding after a container has shipped. A distributor who welcomes these questions is generally one you can work with for years.
## Payment terms and building a second order

Ask about payment terms early, because they shape your cash flow more than the unit price does. Many suppliers ask for a deposit before production and the balance before shipping. Some offer credit after a few successful orders. Find out what the terms are for the first order, what unlocks better terms, and whether there is any discount for earlier payment. A supplier who is flexible here is often easier to grow with than one who insists on full payment upfront forever.

Think about the second order while you are placing the first. A distributor who can tell you which products reorder most often, which have the longest lead time, and which are being discontinued is thinking about your business rather than just this shipment. Ask what the typical reorder cycle looks like for a buyer in your market. If they have no answer, you may be dealing with someone who moves goods rather than builds ranges — fine for a one-off, less useful if you plan to still be here in three years.

Finally, start small enough that a mistake is survivable. The temptation on a first order is to fill a container because the unit price looks better. Resist it. A smaller mixed order teaches you which products actually sell, how the packaging holds up in transit, and whether the supplier does what they said they would. You can always scale up once you have answers. Most of the expensive lessons in wholesale come from ordering with confidence before you have evidence, and almost none come from ordering too little.

posts.title: Looking at a Carhartt dog jacket? Here's what to compare before you buy
posts.excerpt: Carhartt makes tough workwear, so it is natural to look at their dog jacket when you want something that survives winter. The name carries a promise of durabili
body: Carhartt makes tough workwear, so it is natural to look at their dog jacket when you want something that survives winter. The name carries a promise of durability, and for a working dog in a cold climate that promise is attractive. But a jacket for a person on a building site and a jacket for a dog solve different problems. Before you buy on the name alone, here is what is actually worth comparing.
## Durability means different things on a dog

A human work jacket takes abrasion at the elbows, cuffs and knees. A dog jacket takes it at the chest, the belly, and wherever a harness rubs across the shoulders. Heavy canvas sounds ideal, but if it is too stiff it will chafe behind the legs and restrict your dog's stride. A dog does not care how rugged the fabric looks; they care whether they can move normally.

So look at the underside and the leg openings, not just the outer shell. That is where the real wear happens. A tough outer layer paired with a softer, smoother lining at the contact points is usually better than heavy material throughout. Check how the edges are finished too — raw or stiff edging will rub a hole in your dog's coat long before the fabric itself wears out.

There is also weight to consider. A jacket that is robust enough for a construction site can be genuinely heavy once it is wet. Your dog carries that weight for the whole walk, and small dogs feel it disproportionately. Durability that makes the jacket miserable to wear is not durability worth paying for.
## Insulation that works when damp

Winter walks mean wet snow, slush, and damp ground. A jacket filled with PP cotton keeps its loft better than cheap stuffing when it gets slightly wet, and it dries faster afterwards. Compare the fill, not just the outer fabric — a famous name on a label tells you nothing about what is inside.

Down is warmer for its weight, but it loses most of its insulating value when it gets properly wet and takes a long time to dry. If your dog treats every puddle as a personal challenge, that is a realistic failure mode. Synthetic fills like PP cotton are the sensible compromise for most dogs: slightly bulkier, far more forgiving, and easier to wash. Our [Winter Jacket with PP Cotton](/products/pth-1502.html) is built around that decision, with a three-proof shell and a reflective strip for the practical parts of a winter walk.

I am not claiming it is the same thing as a Carhartt dog jacket. It is not, and the brands are not trying to solve identical problems. What I am saying is that fill, shell and construction are the things to compare, and they matter more than the logo on the chest.
## The four-point checklist

When you are standing in a shop or reading two product pages side by side, reduce it to four questions. First, what is the outer shell made of, and are the seams sealed? Second, what is the fill, and how does it behave when damp? Third, where is the reflective material and is it stitched or printed? Fourth, how do the leg openings and chest strap keep the jacket in place when your dog actually moves?

If you cannot find clear answers to all four, the product page is not doing its job, regardless of the brand. A reputable supplier will tell you the materials and the construction because those are the reasons to buy. Marketing copy that talks about heritage and toughness without listing a single material is not giving you anything to compare.

Then measure your dog and check the size chart against those numbers. Back length from the base of the neck to the base of the tail, and chest circumference at the widest point. Do not buy on breed alone — two dogs of the same breed can differ enormously in build. A jacket that is slightly too small in the chest will be taken off at the first opportunity, however good the brand.
## Visibility and fit beat branding

If you walk early or late, a reflective strip matters more than a logo. Dogs are low, and in winter they are often dark. A strip along the back or down the sides gives drivers a chance to see you both from a distance. Printed silver looks good for a season and then fades; stitched reflective thread lasts much longer.

Fit matters more too. A jacket that rides up or twists will be abandoned by your dog within ten minutes, usually while you are standing in a park looking for a dog who has quietly removed their coat. Check that the chest strap closes snugly without restricting breathing, and that the leg openings sit where they should when your dog is standing still and when they are walking.

There is a simple test at home. Put the jacket on, let your dog walk around the house for five minutes, and watch what happens. If it shifts even once, the fit is wrong. If your dog stops and shakes, something is uncomfortable. A jacket that passes this test is worth far more than one with a prestigious label that fails it.
## Price, value and what you are really paying for

A branded jacket costs more, and part of that is the name. That is not automatically bad — a brand with a reputation has an incentive to avoid obvious failures, and you are paying for the testing and support behind the product. But the premium should buy you something concrete: better materials, better construction, better sizing, or a warranty that means something.

Write down the price difference and then check whether it buys a measurable improvement. If the more expensive jacket has the same fill, the same shell, printed rather than stitched reflectives, and the same construction, you are paying for the logo. That may be a choice you are happy to make. Just make it with your eyes open.

Also factor in replacement. A cheaper jacket that lasts one winter and a dearer one that lasts four are not as different as the shelf price suggests. Ask about care and repair — a jacket you can wash without the fill clumping will last longer than one that needs careful handling. The total cost over three seasons is the number that matters.
## Choose for your dog, not the logo

If you love the Carhartt look and it fits your dog well, buy it. There is nothing wrong with wanting a well-made jacket from a brand you trust. But judge any dog jacket on shell, fill, reflectivity and fit. Those four things decide whether your dog is warm and comfortable on a January walk, and none of them are printed on the tag.
## Trying it on without making it a battle

Some dogs accept a jacket immediately. Others treat it like a personal insult. If yours is in the second group, put the jacket on the floor for a day, let them sniff it, and feed a treat near it. Then drape it over their back for a few seconds without fastening anything, and reward. Only once that is boring should you do up the first strap. Build up over several short sessions rather than one long one. A dog who has chosen to tolerate the jacket will keep it on; a dog who has been overpowered into it will find a way to remove it the moment your back is turned.

Check the fit again after a week of real use. Dogs put on and lose weight, winter coats grow in, and straps stretch slightly. A jacket that was perfect in November can be rubbing by January. A quick check of the chest strap and the leg openings once a week takes seconds and prevents the slow discomfort that leads to a dog refusing to wear it at all.

Storage matters more than people expect as well. A wet jacket stuffed into a bag in the hallway will smell within a day and the fill will stay clumped. Hang it somewhere with air moving, ideally away from direct heat, until it is completely dry. If it has picked up mud or road salt, spot-clean it before storing rather than letting it set. A jacket cared for this way looks and performs properly for several winters, which changes the cost calculation considerably when you are weighing it against a cheaper option.

One last consideration is what your dog actually does in winter. A dog who walks steadily for an hour needs more insulation than one who dashes outside for ten minutes and comes back to a warm kitchen. A dog who waits at the door in the rain while you clip on a lead does not need a jacket at all — they need a faster owner. Be honest about your own routine before you spend money on features. The best winter jacket is the one that matches the walks you really take, not the ones you imagine taking in January.

Try the jacket on at home if you can, keep the packaging until you are sure about the size, and give your dog a few minutes to move around in it before you commit. The right jacket becomes invisible after the first minute. The wrong one becomes a thing you argue about every morning.
At Poteho we would rather you buy the right piece once than replace a cheap one twice. Measure carefully, check the construction, and choose for the way you actually live with your pet.
That is the standard we hold every Poteho product to, and it is why we publish real measurements rather than vague claims.

faq.a: It depends on fit and your climate. Carhartt builds durable outerwear, but the right jacket is the one that fits well, insulates when damp and allows free movement. Compare those features across brands rather than buying on the name alone.

faq.q: How should a dog winter jacket fit?
faq.a: Snug around the chest without restricting breathing, long enough to cover the back but not the tail base, with leg openings that stay put when your dog walks. You should fit two fingers between the jacket and your dog's body.

faq.a: For most dogs, a synthetic fill such as PP cotton is the best compromise: warm, quick-drying and forgiving when damp. Down is lighter and warmer for its weight but performs badly when wet and takes much longer to dry.
